work_title: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
chapter: First Section: Transition from Common Rational Moral Knowledge to Philosophical Knowledge
text: It is impossible to think of anything at all in the world, or even beyond it, that could be considered good without limitation except a good will. Intelligence, wit, judgment, and whatever other talents of the mind one might name, or courage, resoluteness, and perseverance as qualities of temperament, are undoubtedly good and desirable for many purposes, but they can also be extremely evil and harmful if the will that makes use of these natural gifts is not good.

work_title: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
chapter: Second Section: The Categorical Imperative (Formula of Universal Law)
text: There is only a single categorical imperative and it is this: Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law. If now from this one imperative all imperatives of duty can be derived as from their principle, we shall be able to show what we understand by duty and what this concept means.

work_title: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
chapter: Second Section: The Formula of Humanity as an End in Itself
text: The practical imperative will thus be the following: Act in such a way that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, never merely as a means to an end, but always at the same time as an end. Rational beings are called persons because their nature already marks them out as ends in themselves, that is, as something which ought not to be used merely as a means.

work_title: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
chapter: Second Section: The Kingdom of Ends and Autonomy
text: A rational being belongs as a member to the kingdom of ends when he gives universal laws in it but is also himself subject to these laws. Autonomy of the will is the property that the will has of being a law to itself (independently of any property of the objects of volition). If the will seeks the law that is to determine it anywhere else than in the fitness of its maxims for its own making of universal law, heteronomy always results.

chapter: Introduction: Distinction Between Pure and Empirical Knowledge
text: There can be no doubt that all our knowledge begins with experience. For how should our faculty of knowledge be awakened into action did not objects affecting our senses partly of themselves produce representations? But though all our knowledge begins with experience, it by no means follows that all arises out of experience. It may well be that even our empirical knowledge is a compound of what we receive through impressions and of what our own faculty of knowledge supplies from itself.

Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe, the more often and steadily we reflect upon them: the starry heavens above me and the moral law within me. I do not need to search for them and merely conjecture them as though they were veiled in obscurity or in the transcendent beyond my horizon; I see them before me and connect them immediately with the consciousness of my existence.

work_title: An Answer to the Question: What is Enlightenment?
text: Enlightenment is man's emergence from his self-incurred immaturity. Immaturity is the inability to use one's own understanding without guidance from another. This immaturity is self-incurred if its cause is not lack of understanding, but lack of resolution and courage to use it without the guidance of another. Sapere aude! Have courage to use your own reason!—that is the motto of enlightenment.
